subject: Polity
description: Article 51A, 42nd & 86th Amendments, count, judicial enforcement, comparison with FRs

questions.stem: Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the:
questions.explanation: Fundamental Duties added by 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — based on Sardar Swaran Singh Committee's recommendations during the Emergency. Inserted Part IV-A (Article 51A). Inspired by USSR Constitution. Originally 10 duties; an 11th was added by 86th Amendment, 2002 (parents to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6-14). Total: 11 Fundamental Duties as of today.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Currently, the number of Fundamental Duties enumerated in Article 51A is:
questions.explanation: 11 — original 10 (a-j) + one added (k) by 86th Amendment 2002. (k) = 'who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years' (linked to Right to Education, Article 21A). The numbering uses lowercase letters (a) to (k). Fundamental Duties are listed as a single article — Article 51A — with no separate sub-articles.

options.option_text: Non-justiciable but courts can refer to them when interpreting laws
Enforceable only against citizens, not state

questions.explanation: Fundamental Duties are NON-justiciable — no direct legal remedy if not performed. Like DPSPs, they are moral obligations. However, courts have used FDs to interpret existing laws (AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS, 2002 — gave them weight equal to DPSPs in constitutional interpretation). Some duties have legislative backing — Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955. Punjab and Haryana HC ruled (2003) that protecting environment is enforceable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the 11 Fundamental Duties under Article 51A?

options.option_text: To safeguard public property and abjure violence
To protect and improve the natural environment
To develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry

questions.explanation: Paying tax is a LEGAL duty (under Income Tax Act) but NOT a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A. The 11 FDs cover: respect Constitution, anthem, flag, abide by ideals; cherish freedom-struggle ideals; protect sovereignty, integrity, unity; defend country & render national service; promote harmony & brotherhood, renounce derogatory practices to women's dignity; preserve culture; protect environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property + abjure violence; strive towards excellence; provide education to one's child (added 2002).

questions.stem: Which committee, in 1999, recommended introducing Fundamental Duties into the school curriculum and operationalising them?
questions.explanation: Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) — appointed by the Centre — recommended teaching Fundamental Duties through education + enforcement via existing laws + identifying laws connected to each duty. Found that 11 of the 11 FDs are reflected in some existing law. Recommended a 'National Foundation for Fundamental Rights and Duties'. Sarkaria — Centre-State relations (1988); Punchhi — Centre-State (2010); Liberhan — Babri Masjid demolition (2009).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Fundamental Duty to 'develop scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry' was inspired by:
questions.explanation: Article 51A(h) — 'to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.' Reflects Nehru's vision articulated in 'Discovery of India' (1946). Term 'scientific temper' was coined by Nehru himself. Nehru wanted India to embrace rational thinking, evidence-based reasoning. The phrase is invoked frequently in court judgements opposing superstition (e.g., banning of dolphin shows, witch-hunting laws). Maharashtra Anti-Superstition Act (2013) draws from this duty.

questions.stem: Among major democracies, only one country alongside India explicitly enshrines a list of citizen duties. That country is:

options.option_text: USSR (now Russian Federation; the original FD-list inspiration)

questions.explanation: Soviet Constitution (1977) had Articles 60-69 listing duties of Soviet citizens. India's Swaran Singh Committee (1976) drew inspiration from it. After USSR dissolution, the Russian Federation Constitution (1993) retained some duties. Other democracies — US, UK, Australia, Canada — do not have explicit constitutional duty lists; civic obligations exist via ordinary laws. Japan, China, Vietnam, Cuba have constitutional duties. India is one of the few major democracies with this feature.
